l: blessedness and prosperity, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 2
s: Those who keep the commandments of God are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual. If they remain faithful to the end, they are received into heaven to dwell with God in never-ending happiness, and they prosper in the land.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The angel tells the people that the Lord Omnipotent will come among them as Jesus Christ, perform miracles, suffer, die, and rise again. Jesus Christ’s blood atones for the sins of those who died without knowing God’s will, while salvation comes only through repentance and faith in his name. The people, prophets, and law of Moses testify of Christ’s coming, but the natural man remains an enemy to God unless he yields to the Holy Spirit. At the judgment, people are judged according to their works, and the wicked are consigned to misery, torment, and damnation.

l: the angel, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The angel comes from God and declares glad tidings to the speaker. He teaches about the coming of the Lord Omnipotent, salvation through Jesus Christ, judgment, and the fate of the wicked.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: God sends the angel and holy prophets among all the children of men. God’s will concerns the sins and salvation of those who do not know it or who sin ignorantly.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The Lord Omnipotent reigns from all eternity to all eternity and will come down from heaven among the children of men in a tabernacle of clay. He will work mighty miracles, judge the world, and provide salvation through his atoning blood.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ is called the Son of God, the Father of heaven and earth, and the Creator of all things from the beginning. He comes among his own, is rejected and crucified, and provides salvation through faith on his name.

l: Adam, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Adam’s transgression causes people to fall and die. His fall is used as an example of justice and the consequences of partaking of forbidden fruit.

l: Spirit of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The Holy Spirit entices the natural man to yield, put off the natural man, and become a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The people are taught about the coming of Christ, salvation, repentance, faith, and judgment. They are described as stiffnecked, and they harden their hearts and fail to understand that the law of Moses has value only through Christ’s atonement.

l: the prophets, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Holy prophets declare the coming of Christ to every kindred, nation, and tongue. They speak of his coming through signs, wonders, types, and shadows.

l: little children, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Little children are blessed, and the blood of Christ atones for their sins. An infant who dies in infancy does not perish, and little children are the only ones described as blameless before God.

l: the natural man, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The natural man is an enemy to God from the fall of Adam and will remain so unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit. He must put off the natural man and become as a submissive, meek, humble, patient, loving child.

l: the law of Moses, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The law of Moses is appointed to the people because they are stiffnecked. It is shown through signs, wonders, types, and shadows, but it avails nothing except through the atonement of Christ’s blood.

l: coming of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The coming of Christ is declared by an angel, prophets, signs, wonders, types, and shadows. The Lord Omnipotent will come among the children of men, and knowledge of the Savior will eventually spread throughout every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.

l: the ministry of Jesus Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ will work mighty miracles, including healing the sick, raising the dead, causing the lame to walk, restoring sight to the blind, enabling the deaf to hear, curing diseases, and casting out devils.

l: the crucifixion and death of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ will suffer temptation, pain, hunger, thirst, fatigue, and anguish so great that blood will come from every pore. He will be considered a man, accused of having a devil, scourged, and crucified.

l: the resurrection of the dead, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ will rise from the dead on the third day. After this, he will stand to judge the world.

l: the Atonement of Jesus Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The blood of Jesus Christ atones for the sins of those who died without knowing God’s will or who sinned ignorantly. Salvation, including the blessing of infants and little children, comes through his atoning blood.

l: the Fall of Adam, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The Fall of Adam causes people to fall by nature and provides the condition from which the natural man is an enemy to God. It is compared with Adam’s partaking of the forbidden fruit, which justice could not deny.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Salvation comes only through the name of Jesus Christ, the Lord Omnipotent. It comes through repentance and faith, and no other name, way, or means can provide it.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Sin includes rebellion against God, transgression, ignorance, and the wickedness and abominations of the people. Those who knowingly rebel cannot receive salvation except through repentance and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

l: repentance and faith, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Repentance and faith on the Lord Jesus Christ are required for salvation. People must humble themselves, become as little children, and believe in salvation through Christ’s atoning blood.

l: Final Judgment, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ will stand to judge the world, and every person will be judged according to his or her works. The people taught these words will stand as a bright testimony against the people at the judgment day.

l: everlasting punishment, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: Those who refuse to humble themselves and become as little children drink damnation to their own souls. The wicked are consigned to an awful view of their guilt and abominations, misery, endless torment, and a lake of fire and brimstone.

l: hell, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 3
s: The wicked are described as entering a state of misery and endless torment from which they can no more return. Their torment is compared to a lake of fire and brimstone with unquenchable flames and smoke ascending forever and ever.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: King Benjamin teaches the people about salvation through the atonement of Jesus Christ, repentance, faith, and obedience to the commandments of God. The people receive a remission of their sins and peace of conscience through their faith in Jesus Christ. He teaches that all people depend upon God and must care for the poor, beggar, and needy by sharing their substance wisely and in order. He warns that those who fail to watch their thoughts, words, deeds, and obedience to God must perish.

l: king Benjamin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: King Benjamin teaches the people about the goodness and power of God, salvation through the atonement, repentance, faith, and obedience. He commands them to remember their dependence on God, care for the poor, and continue in faith concerning the coming of the Lord.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The Lord sends an angel whose words king Benjamin delivers to the people. The Lord grants forgiveness and pours out his Spirit upon those who call on him in faith and sincerity.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: Jesus Christ is identified as the one in whom the people believe and through whose atonement salvation and forgiveness are received. He is to come down among the children of men.

l: Son of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The people believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth and all things and shall come among the children of men.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: God created all things and has all wisdom and power. People depend on him for their lives and possessions, and he grants right requests made in faith.

l: man, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: Man is described as having a carnal, worthless, fallen, and dependent state. He must believe, repent, humble himself, watch his thoughts, words, and deeds, and share his substance according to what he has.

l: poor, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The poor who have sufficient to remain from day to day are taught to remain guiltless by desiring to give if they had more. Those who covet what they have not received are condemned.

l: beggar, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The beggar may ask for substance so that he does not perish. Those who deny him when they have the means to help are condemned.

l: kingdom of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: A person who refuses to help someone in misery has great cause to repent and, unless he repents, perishes forever and has no interest in the kingdom of God.

l: the Atonement of Jesus Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The atonement was prepared from the foundation of the world so that salvation might come to those who trust in the Lord, diligently keep his commandments, and continue in faith to the end of mortal life.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: Salvation comes through the atonement prepared for all mankind since the fall of Adam. No other salvation or conditions for salvation are given besides those taught by king Benjamin.

l: remission of sins, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The people receive a remission of their sins after calling on God in faith, and they experience joy and peace of conscience. They are taught to retain a remission of their sins by remembering God, remaining humble, praying daily, and serving others.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: Sin includes failing to repent, refusing to help those in need, borrowing without returning what was agreed upon, and failing to watch one's thoughts, words, and deeds while neglecting God's commandments.

l: faith, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: Faith in Jesus Christ brings forgiveness, joy, and peace of conscience. People must continue in faith concerning what they have heard about the coming of the Lord until the end of their lives.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: People must repent of their sins, forsake them, humble themselves before God, and ask sincerely for forgiveness. Those who refuse to repent after withholding help from the needy perish forever.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: People are instructed to observe the commandments of God and continue in faith to the end of their lives. Failure to do so results in perishing.

l: goodness of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: Knowledge of the goodness of God awakens people to their nothingness and fallen state. His goodness, power, wisdom, patience, and long-suffering are to be remembered continually.

l: substance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: People receive their substance from God and are taught to impart it to one another. They should use it to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and administer relief according to the needy person's wants, with wisdom and order.

l: coming of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: The people are to continue in faith concerning the coming of the Lord, which was spoken by the mouth of the angel. They must remain faithful to the end of their lives.

l: care for the needy, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 4
s: People are commanded to succor those in need, give them substance, and not allow the beggar to ask in vain. This care includes feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and providing spiritual and temporal relief according to their wants.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: King Benjamin’s people affirm that they believe his words because the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent has wrought a mighty change in their hearts, removing their disposition to do evil and giving them a desire to do good. They enter into a covenant with God to do his will and obey his commandments throughout their lives. King Benjamin teaches that through this covenant they become children of Christ, take upon themselves the name of Christ, and may receive salvation and eternal life if they remain steadfast and abound in good works.

l: king Benjamin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: King Benjamin sends among his people to learn whether they believe his words. He accepts their covenant as righteous and teaches them about becoming children of Christ, taking upon themselves the name of Christ, and remaining steadfast in good works.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: Christ spiritually begets those who enter into a covenant with God and have changed hearts through faith on his name. He may seal them as his and bring them to heaven.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: God is the one with whom king Benjamin’s people covenant to do his will and obey his commandments. His name is associated with the right and left hands, and he is described as the creator of all things and God above all.

l: Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: The Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent works a mighty change in king Benjamin’s people, changing their hearts and removing their disposition to do evil.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: King Benjamin’s people believe his words, know their truth through the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, and rejoice with exceedingly great joy. They covenant to do God’s will, obey his commandments, take upon themselves the name of Christ, and remain steadfast in good works.

l: children of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: Those who make the covenant with God are called the children of Christ, his sons and daughters, because Christ spiritually begets them and their hearts are changed through faith on his name.

l: covenant, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: The covenant with God is a commitment to do his will and obey his commandments for the remainder of one’s days. King Benjamin calls it a righteous covenant and connects it with becoming children of Christ.

l: faith, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: Faith in the things king Benjamin has spoken brings his people to great knowledge and exceedingly great joy. Faith on Christ’s name changes their hearts and makes them his sons and daughters.

l: mighty change of heart, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: The mighty change of heart is wrought by the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent. It removes the disposition to do evil and gives king Benjamin’s people a disposition to do good continually.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: King Benjamin’s people covenant to obey God’s commandments in all things that God commands them, throughout the remainder of their days.

l: the name of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: Those who covenant with God are instructed to take upon themselves the name of Christ and retain it in their hearts. The name should not be blotted out except through transgression, and knowing it determines whether a person is found at the right or left hand of God.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: There is no other name given whereby salvation comes. Salvation is described as everlasting and is received through Christ’s wisdom, power, justice, and mercy.

l: eternal life, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: Eternal life is promised with everlasting salvation to those who are brought to heaven through Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent.

l: evil, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 5
s: King Benjamin’s people say that the change wrought in them has removed their disposition to do evil and made them desire to do good continually. They are also instructed to remain steadfast and abound in good works.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: King Benjamin finishes speaking to the people, takes the names of those who entered into a covenant with God, and consecrates his son Mosiah as ruler and king. The people covenant to keep God's commandments and take upon themselves the name of Christ, except for little children. Mosiah begins to reign, appoints priests to teach the people, and tills the earth so he will not become burdensome to them. King Benjamin lives three years after these events and then dies.

l: king Benjamin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: King Benjamin finishes speaking to the people, takes the names of those who entered into a covenant with God, consecrates Mosiah as ruler and king, gives him charges concerning the kingdom, appoints priests, and dismisses the multitude. He lives three years and then dies.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: The people enter into a covenant with God to keep his commandments and take upon themselves the name of Christ, except for little children. They return to their own houses according to their families, and there is no contention among them for three years.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: God is the one with whom the people enter into a covenant, promising to keep his commandments.

l: covenant, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: The covenant is entered into by all the people except little children, and it concerns keeping God's commandments and taking upon themselves the name of Christ.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: The people who enter into the covenant take upon themselves the name of Christ.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 6
s: Mosiah is consecrated by king Benjamin as ruler and king, receives charges concerning the kingdom, and begins to reign in his father's stead at thirty years of age. He walks in the ways of the Lord, keeps God's commandments, appoints priests to teach the people, and tills the earth so he will not become burdensome to them.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: King Mosiah sends Ammon and fifteen other strong men from the land of Zarahemla to inquire about the people who went to dwell in the land of Lehi-Nephi. Ammon and three companions are captured near the land of Nephi and brought before Limhi, who learns that their brethren in Zarahemla are alive. Limhi explains that his people are in bondage to the Lamanites and pay half of their produce, flocks, herds, and possessions as tribute. He teaches that their iniquities and transgressions brought affliction upon them, but promises that God will deliver them if they turn to him and serve him diligently.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: King Mosiah had continual peace for three years and was troubled by questions about the people who had gone to the land of Lehi-Nephi. He permitted sixteen strong men, led by Ammon, to go up and inquire concerning their brethren.

l: the people of Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The people who went up to dwell in the land of Lehi-Nephi had sent no word to the people of Zarahemla since leaving. Their absence caused king Mosiah’s people to question him continually.

l: land of Lehi-Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The land of Lehi-Nephi was the destination of Ammon and the sixteen men from Zarahemla. Ammon and his companions did not know the route and wandered in the wilderness for forty days before reaching the area.

l: city of Lehi-Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The city of Lehi-Nephi was among the possessions yielded by king Laman to Zeniff. It was held by Limhi’s people, who were in bondage to the Lamanites.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The land of Zarahemla sent Ammon and fifteen other strong men to inquire about the people who had left. Ammon said he was a descendant of Zarahemla and had come from this land.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: Ammon led sixteen men from the land of Zarahemla to inquire about their brethren. He and Amaleki, Helem, and Hem were captured, imprisoned, and brought before Limhi; after identifying himself, he was released and welcomed.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The land of Nephi was the place where Ammon and three of his brethren went down after reaching the hill north of Shilom. There they met the king’s guard and were taken prisoner.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: Limhi was the son of Noah and grandson of Zeniff, and he had been made king by the voice of the people. He questioned Ammon, learned that the people of Zarahemla were alive, and encouraged his people to trust in God for deliverance.

l: Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: Zeniff came up from the land of Zarahemla to inherit the land of his fathers and was made king over the people. His over-zealousness led him to be deceived by king Laman and to yield the cities of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The people of Limhi were in bondage to the Lamanites and paid a grievous tribute. Limhi gathered them at the temple and taught that their iniquities had brought their afflictions, while urging them to turn to God.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The Lamanites held the people of Limhi in bondage and exacted half of their corn, barley, grain, flocks, herds, possessions, or lives as tribute. King Laman deceived Zeniff in order to bring the people into subjection.

l: Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: Limhi said that it would be better for his people to be slaves to the Nephites than to pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites. He expected their brethren to deliver them from bondage.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The people of Limhi were in bondage to the Lamanites because of their iniquities and abominations. Limhi taught that God would deliver them from bondage if they turned to him with full purpose of heart and served him diligently.

l: taxation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The people of Limhi paid the Lamanites half of their corn, barley, grain, flocks, herds, and possessions, or their lives. Limhi described this tribute as grievous to bear.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: God brought the children of Israel out of Egypt, preserved the fathers of Limhi’s people, and had kept his people until that time. Limhi taught that God could deliver his people from bondage if they trusted and served him.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The iniquities and abominations of Limhi’s people caused God to bring them into bondage. Their iniquities were also connected to the shedding of blood and their afflictions.

l: affliction, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The people of Limhi suffered great affliction, including bondage, tribute, and the deaths of many brethren. Limhi said their affliction resulted from transgression and gave them reason to mourn.

l: prophet of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: A prophet of the Lord was slain after warning the people about their wickedness and abominations. He prophesied of many things to come, including the coming of Christ.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The Lord would not succor his people in the day of their transgression and would hedge up their ways so that they did not prosper. He promised destruction and affliction for those who sowed filthiness, but also promised deliverance if his people turned to him.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: Christ was taught by the slain prophet to be the God and Father of all things who would take upon himself the image of man, flesh, and blood. The teaching about Christ led the people to put the prophet to death.

l: coming of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The prophet of the Lord prophesied of the coming of Christ. The people killed him because he taught that Christ would come among the children of men and take upon himself flesh and blood.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The people’s transgression led to their bondage and affliction. The Lord would not succor them while they remained in transgression.

l: promise of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: The promise of the Lord was fulfilled when the people were smitten and afflicted because of their wickedness. The Lord also promised that he would deliver them if they turned to him and served him with diligence.

l: deliverance from bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 7
s: Limhi taught that deliverance from bondage was near if the people trusted in God. He said that God would deliver them according to his own will and pleasure if they turned to him with full purpose of heart and served him diligently.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: King Limhi tells his people about their brethren in the land of Zarahemla, and Ammon recounts what happened from Zeniff’s departure until Ammon’s arrival. Limhi’s people present plates, breastplates, and swords from a discovered land filled with bones and ruins, but no one can interpret the plates. Ammon explains that the king of the people in the land of Zarahemla is a seer who can translate ancient records through interpreters, a gift from God. Limhi rejoices because the records may reveal the identity and destruction of the people who made them.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: King Limhi tells his people about their brethren in the land of Zarahemla and has Ammon recount their history. He presents the plates containing the record of his people to Ammon and asks about translating the records.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: Ammon rehearses the history of Limhi’s brethren and explains king Benjamin’s words to Limhi’s people. He says that the king of the people in the land of Zarahemla can translate ancient records because he is a seer.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The people of king Limhi hear Ammon recount the history of their brethren and the words of king Benjamin. They possess records and artifacts brought back from a discovered land.

l: brethren in the land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The brethren in the land of Zarahemla are the people whose history Ammon recounts to Limhi’s people, from the time Zeniff left until Ammon came up out of Limhi’s land.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The king of the people in the land of Zarahemla is the man commanded to use the interpreters and possesses a high gift from God. He is a seer, revelator, and prophet who can translate ancient records.

l: forty-three people sent into the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: Forty-three people were sent into the wilderness to find the land of Zarahemla and appeal to Limhi’s brethren for deliverance from bondage. They became lost, traveled in a land among many waters, and returned to Limhi’s land after discovering another land.

l: people who had been destroyed, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The people who had been destroyed had populated the discovered land in numbers as great as the hosts of Israel. Their land contained bones, ruins of buildings, and records whose translation might reveal who they were and why they were destroyed.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The land of Zarahemla was the destination sought by the forty-three people sent into the wilderness. They did not find it, and Ammon identifies its king as the person able to translate the ancient records.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: Limhi’s land was where the forty-three people returned after failing to find the land of Zarahemla. Ammon came up out of this land, and the plates containing its people’s record were brought before him.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The forty-three people traveled through the wilderness for many days while seeking the land of Zarahemla. They were lost but remained diligent and eventually returned to Limhi’s land.

l: discovered land of the destroyed people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The discovered land was covered with bones of men and beasts, ruins of buildings, and artifacts. It had been populated by a numerous people who were later destroyed.

l: plates containing the record of Limhi's people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The plates containing the record of Limhi’s people were brought before Ammon so he could read them. Their record was made from the time Limhi’s people left the land of Zarahemla.

l: plates of gold, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The twenty-four plates were brought back from the discovered land as evidence of what the forty-three people reported. They were filled with engravings and made of pure gold, but no one in the land could interpret them.

l: interpreters, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The interpreters are instruments through which ancient records can be translated. Ammon says no one may look in them unless commanded, and Limhi believes they were prepared to unfold mysteries to the children of men.

l: seer, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: A seer is a revelator and a prophet who can know things that are past and things that are to come. Through a seer, secret and hidden things can be revealed and otherwise unknown things can be made known.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: God gives a man great power and the gift to translate ancient records through interpreters. God has provided a means for people to work mighty miracles through faith.

l: journey to find the land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The journey was undertaken by forty-three people who hoped to find the land of Zarahemla and ask Limhi’s brethren to deliver them from bondage. They were lost for many days, failed to find Zarahemla, and returned after discovering another land.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The bondage of Limhi’s people motivated the forty-three people to seek the land of Zarahemla and appeal to their brethren for deliverance.

l: destruction of the people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The destruction of the people who had inhabited the discovered land is a subject Limhi wants to understand. He hopes the translated records will reveal its cause.

l: translation of the records, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 8
s: The translation of the records is desired by king Limhi because it may reveal the identity and destruction of the people who made them. Ammon says the king of the people in the land of Zarahemla can translate them through the interpreters.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: Zeniff leads a group from Zarahemla into the wilderness and obtains permission from king Laman to possess the land of Lehi-Nephi and the land of Shilom. Zeniff’s people build, repair walls, cultivate crops, and prosper, but king Laman intends to bring them into bondage. After twelve years, king Laman stirs up the Lamanites, who attack Zeniff’s people and take their flocks and crops. Zeniff arms his people, prays to God, and leads them to defeat the Lamanites, although 279 of his people are killed.

l: Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: Zeniff is sent as a spy among the Lamanites but desires that they not be destroyed after seeing what is good among them. He leads people to possess the land, secures king Laman’s permission to occupy the land of Lehi-Nephi and the land of Shilom, and later leads his people in battle against the Lamanites.

l: Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: The Nephites include Zeniff’s brethren and army, among whom father fought against father and brother against brother until many were destroyed. Zeniff’s people return to the land of Zarahemla, later settle in the land of Nephi, and fight against the Lamanites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: The Lamanites are described as lazy and idolatrous and as desiring to bring Zeniff’s people into bondage. They attack Zeniff’s people, take flocks and crops, and are driven out of the land after losing 3,043 people.

l: king Laman, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: King Laman covenants with Zeniff that Zeniff may possess the land of Lehi-Nephi and the land of Shilom, and commands his people to depart. His action is described as cunning and crafty because he intends to bring Zeniff’s people into bondage, and he later stirs up his people to contend with them.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: God hears the cries and answers the prayers of Zeniff and his people when they ask for deliverance from their enemies. His strength enables them to go forth against the Lamanites and drive them out of the land.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: Zeniff’s people journey to and settle in the land of Nephi. In the thirteenth year of Zeniff’s reign there, the Lamanites attack his people south of the land of Shilom.

l: land of Lehi-Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: King Laman allows Zeniff to possess the land of Lehi-Nephi and commands his people to leave it. Zeniff and his people enter and possess the land.

l: land of Shilom, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: King Laman allows Zeniff to possess the land of Shilom and commands his people to depart. Zeniff’s people build and repair the walls of the city of Shilom and cultivate the surrounding land.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: King Laman intends to bring Zeniff’s people into bondage so that his people can benefit from the labor of their hands and the flocks of their fields. After twelve years, the threat of bondage contributes to the conflict between the peoples.

l: wars and contentions, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: Wars and contentions begin in the land after king Laman stirs up his people against Zeniff’s people. The conflict includes an attack on Zeniff’s people and a battle in which the Lamanites are driven out.

l: Lamanite attack, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 9
s: In the thirteenth year of Zeniff’s reign, a numerous host of Lamanites attacks Zeniff’s people while they water and feed their flocks and till their lands. The attackers slay people and take flocks and corn, but Zeniff and his people defeat them after praying to God.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff and his people establish and possess their land in peace for twenty-two years, preparing weapons, guarding the land, farming, and making cloth. After king Laman dies, his son stirs the Lamanites to war, but Zeniff’s spies discover their preparations and Zeniff organizes his people for battle. Zeniff teaches his people about the Lamanites’ traditions and urges them to trust in the Lord, enabling them to drive the Lamanites from the land with a great slaughter. Being old, Zeniff confers the kingdom upon one of his sons.

l: Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff establishes the kingdom, prepares weapons and guards, and organizes his people for defense. In his old age, he leads them into battle, teaches them about the Lamanites, urges them to trust in the Lord, and later confers the kingdom upon one of his sons.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: The Lamanites prepare for war after king Laman dies, coming with numerous hosts armed with bows, arrows, swords, cimeters, stones, and slings. They are described as wild, ferocious, and blood-thirsty, with an eternal hatred towards the children of Nephi, but Zeniff’s people drive them from the land and kill many of them.

l: Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff’s people possess their land in peace for twenty-two years, farming, tending flocks, making cloth, and preparing weapons. They hide their women and children, gather their able men for battle, trust in the Lord, defeat the Lamanites, and return to their land.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: The Lord protects Zeniff’s people as they go to battle in his strength. The Lamanites do not know the Lord or his strength, while Nephi was favored because the Lord heard and answered his prayers.

l: king Laman, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: King Laman dies, and his son begins to reign in his stead. Before his death, king Laman deceived Zeniff through cunning, lying craftiness, and fair promises, leading Zeniff’s people into the land so they could be destroyed.

l: Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Nephi was more faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord, so the Lord favored him, heard his prayers, and answered them. Nephi led the journey in the wilderness, departed into the wilderness as commanded, and took the records engraved on the plates of brass.

l: the people of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: The Lamanites teach their children to hate, murder, rob, plunder, and destroy the children of Nephi. They therefore maintain an eternal hatred towards the children of Nephi.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: The land is inherited by Zeniff’s people for twenty-two years, during which they prosper and have continual peace. The Lamanites attack it, but Zeniff’s people drive them out and return to it.

l: possession of the land in peace, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff and his people again begin to establish the kingdom and possess the land in peace. This peaceful possession lasts for twenty-two years before the Lamanites prepare to attack.

l: preparations for war, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff causes weapons of every kind to be made and sets guards around the land to detect and prevent Lamanite attacks. After king Laman dies, his son stirs the Lamanites to rebellion and they prepare for war, while Zeniff’s spies discover their preparations.

l: battle against the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff’s people hide their women and children, gather their able men, arrange them by age, and go to battle against the Lamanites in the strength of the Lord. They contend face to face and drive the Lamanites out of the land.

l: slaughter of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 10
s: Zeniff’s people slay the Lamanites with a great slaughter, killing so many that they do not number them. They then return to their own land.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Zeniff confers the kingdom upon his son Noah, who reigns wickedly, taxes the people heavily, supports priests and lavish building, and leads the people into sin, idolatry, and violence. The Lamanites attack Noah's people, and Noah's armies drive them back in a victory that causes pride and delight in blood. Abinadi prophesies that the Lord will punish the people with affliction and bondage unless they repent and turn to the Lord. Noah and the people harden their hearts against Abinadi and the word of the Lord, and Noah seeks Abinadi's life.

l: Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Zeniff confers the kingdom upon Noah, one of his sons.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah begins to reign in Zeniff's stead but does not walk in his father's ways. He taxes the people, supports himself, his wives and concubines, and his priests, builds extensively, lives riotously, and hardens his heart against the word of the Lord. After hearing Abinadi's words, Noah becomes angry and commands that Abinadi be brought to him so that he may slay him.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Abinadi goes among Noah's people and prophesies that the Lord will visit them in anger unless they repent. After the people and Noah seek to take his life, the Lord delivers Abinadi from their hands.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: The Lord commands Abinadi to warn Noah's people to repent and turn to the Lord their God. The Lord declares that he will deliver the people into the hands of their enemies and allow them to suffer affliction if they do not repent, and that he will hear and deliver them if they cry mightily to him after repenting.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: The Lamanites begin entering the land in small numbers, killing Noah's people in their fields and while they tend their flocks. They kill guards, drive many flocks out of the land, and begin to destroy Noah's people and exercise hatred upon them.

l: this people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah's people are taxed to support Noah, his household, and his priests, and they labor exceedingly to support iniquity. They become idolatrous, participate in wickedness and violence, rejoice in victory over the Lamanites, and harden their hearts against Abinadi's words.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah replaces the priests consecrated by his father with new priests lifted up in the pride of their hearts. Noah's priests are supported by the people's taxes, engage in laziness, idolatry, and whoredoms, and speak lying and vain words to the people.

l: land of Shilom, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah builds many buildings in the land of Shilom and builds a tower on the hill north of it. From a tower near the temple, Noah can overlook the land of Shilom.

l: taxation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah lays a tax of one fifth of the people's possessions, including precious metals, other materials, fatlings, and grain. The taxation supports Noah, his wives and concubines, and his priests, and causes the people to labor exceedingly to support iniquity.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah causes his people to commit sin and do what is abominable in the sight of the Lord. The people are deceived by the flattering words of Noah and his priests and become idolatrous.

l: wickedness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah's people commit wickedness, and Abinadi warns that the Lord has seen their wickedness. The Lord threatens to afflict them and deliver them into bondage unless they repent.

l: whoredoms, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah has many wives and concubines and causes the people to commit whoredoms. Noah's priests also spend their time with harlots, and Abinadi identifies the people's whoredoms as a reason for the Lord's warning.

l: victory over the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Noah's armies are sent against the Lamanites and drive them back for a time. After the victory, Noah's people become proud, boast in their strength, and delight in the shedding of blood.

l: words of Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Abinadi's prophecy declares that Noah's people must repent and turn to the Lord or be delivered into the hands of their enemies and brought into bondage. It also states that the Lord will be slow to hear their cries unless they repent in sackcloth and ashes and cry mightily to him.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: The Lord warns through Abinadi that Noah's people will be brought into bondage and afflicted by their enemies if they do not repent. None will deliver them except the Lord the Almighty God.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 11
s: Abinadi calls on Noah's people to repent and turn to the Lord their God. He says they must repent in sackcloth and ashes and cry mightily to the Lord for him to hear their prayers and deliver them.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: Abinadi returns among the people in disguise and prophesies that the Lord will punish them for their iniquities and abominations unless they repent. The people seize Abinadi and bring him before king Noah, who imprisons him and has the priests question him. Abinadi rebukes the priests for failing to understand and keep the law of Moses, and he teaches that obedience to the commandments of God leads to salvation.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: Abinadi comes among the people in disguise and prophesies against them because they have hardened their hearts and failed to repent. He is seized, brought before king Noah, imprisoned, and questioned by the priests, whom he boldly confounds and rebukes.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: King Noah is warned that his life will be afflicted because of his iniquities unless he repents. He causes Abinadi to be imprisoned and orders the priests to question him.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: The Lord commands Abinadi to prophesy against the people because of their hardened hearts, evil doings, iniquities, and abominations. He declares that he will punish them with bondage, afflictions, famine, pestilence, and destruction unless they repent.

l: this people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: This people have hardened their hearts against the Lord's words and have not repented of their evil doings. They become angry with Abinadi, seize him, and bring him before king Noah, and they face prophesied bondage, affliction, and destruction unless they repent.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: The priests question Abinadi in order to accuse him, but he withstands and confounds them. They claim to teach the law of Moses, yet Abinadi says they have not kept it, have set their hearts upon riches, committed whoredoms, and caused the people to sin.

l: the law of Moses, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: The priests say they teach the law of Moses and claim that salvation comes by it. Abinadi challenges them for not keeping it and identifies its commandments, including worshiping no other God and making no graven images.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: Abinadi teaches that people will be saved if they keep the commandments of God delivered to Moses on Mount Sinai. These include having no other God and making no graven image.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: The priests say that salvation comes by the law of Moses. Abinadi teaches that salvation comes through keeping the commandments of God.

l: wickedness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 12
s: The Lord says he will visit the people in anger because of their iniquities and abominations. Their iniquities and abominations are also given as the reason for the prophesied afflictions, pestilence, and destruction.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: Abinadi continues his message to king Noah and the people of king Noah after they cannot kill him because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him. He recites the commandments of God and condemns the priests for teaching iniquity instead of obedience. He explains that the law of Moses was given to a stiffnecked people as a strict law of performances and ordinances, but that salvation does not come by the law alone. He teaches that the atonement, the redemption of God, and the coming Messiah are necessary, and that the Messiah will bring to pass the resurrection of the dead.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: Abinadi finishes his message to king Noah and the people of king Noah after God protects him from being slain. He recites the commandments of God, condemns the people’s iniquities, and teaches about the law of Moses, salvation, the atonement, the Messiah, and the resurrection of the dead.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: King Noah orders his priests to remove and slay Abinadi, calling him mad. Abinadi teaches him that salvation does not come by the law of Moses alone and condemns the iniquity taught under his rule.

l: this people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The people of king Noah cannot lay their hands on Abinadi because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him. They are cut to their hearts, filled with wonder and amazement, and angered because he tells them the truth concerning their iniquities.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: God protects Abinadi from being destroyed before he delivers his message and gives him power and authority to speak. God gives commandments, will make the atonement for the sins and iniquities of his people, and will redeem his people.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The commandments of God include prohibitions against graven images, taking the name of the Lord in vain, breaking the sabbath, dishonoring parents, killing, committing adultery, stealing, bearing false witness, and coveting. Abinadi says the commandments are not written in the people’s hearts.

l: the law of Moses, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The law of Moses was expedient for the children of Israel because they were stiffnecked, quick to do iniquity, and slow to remember the Lord. It consisted of strict performances and ordinances that served as types of things to come, but it would eventually no longer be expedient to keep.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: Abinadi teaches that salvation does not come by the law alone. Without the atonement that God himself shall make, the people would unavoidably perish notwithstanding the law of Moses.

l: the Atonement of Jesus Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The atonement is made by God himself for the sins and iniquities of his people. Without it, they must unavoidably perish even if they keep the law of Moses.

l: Messiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The Messiah is the one concerning whom Moses and the prophets prophesied. He will come among the children of men, take upon him the form of man, and be oppressed and afflicted.

l: redemption, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The redemption of God is necessary because no man can be saved except through it. Abinadi says the children of Israel did not understand this because of the hardness of their hearts.

l: the resurrection of the dead, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 13
s: The resurrection of the dead is among the things prophesied concerning the coming Messiah. Abinadi teaches that the Messiah himself will bring it to pass.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: The unit concerns Isaiah’s prophecy about a suffering servant of the Lord. The servant is despised, rejected, wounded, bruised, oppressed, and led to death for the transgressions, iniquities, and sins of many. He bears griefs and sorrows, makes intercession for transgressors, and justifies many through his knowledge. After offering his soul for sin, he sees his seed, prolongs his days, and receives a portion with the great.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: Isaiah is cited as declaring who has believed the report and to whom the arm of the Lord is revealed. His prophecy describes the servant’s appearance, suffering, death, offering for sin, and eventual portion with the great.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: The Lord’s arm is revealed in the servant’s work. The Lord lays upon the servant the iniquities of all, and the pleasure of the Lord prospers in the servant’s hand.

l: the Lord's servant, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: The Lord’s servant grows up as a tender plant and is despised, rejected, wounded, bruised, oppressed, and afflicted. He bears the griefs, sorrows, iniquities, and sins of many, opens not his mouth before slaughter, makes intercession for transgressors, and is ultimately given a portion with the great.

l: transgressions, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: Transgressions cause the servant to be wounded and stricken. The servant bears the sins of many and makes intercession for transgressors.

l: bonds of iniquity, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: The servant is bruised for iniquities and bears them. The Lord lays the iniquities of all upon him.

l: death, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: The servant makes his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death. He pours out his soul unto death and is numbered with the transgressors.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 14
s: The servant’s soul is made an offering for sin. After this offering, he sees his seed, prolongs his days, and the pleasure of the Lord prospers in his hand.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Abinadi teaches that God shall come down among the children of men as the Son of God and the Father, suffer, die, and redeem his people. The prophets and all who believe their words and look forward to redemption are called the seed of the Lord and heirs of the kingdom of God. The Lord breaks the bands of death, brings the resurrection of the dead, and grants eternal life to those who have part in the first resurrection. Salvation shall be declared to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people, and the Lord shall bring again Zion and redeem Jerusalem.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Abinadi teaches that God shall come down among the children of men, redeem his people, suffer, die, break the bands of death, and bring salvation. He identifies the seed of the Lord, the first resurrection, and the consequences of wilfully rebelling against God.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: God himself shall come down among the children of men and shall redeem his people. God is described as one God, the Eternal Father of heaven and of earth, who breaks the bands of death and brings to pass the resurrection of the dead.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Son of God is God dwelling in flesh and is one with the Father. He suffers temptation, rejection, mocking, scourging, crucifixion, and death, then gains victory over death and makes intercession for the children of men.

l: the Father, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Father is identified with God because the Son was conceived by the power of God. The Son subjects the flesh and his will to the Father, and the Father and the Son are one God.

l: children of men, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The children of men are the people among whom God shall come down. The Son suffers and makes intercession for them, takes upon himself their iniquity and transgressions, and shows compassion toward them.

l: the prophets, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The prophets who have prophesied concerning the coming of the Lord and have not fallen into transgression are the seed of the Lord. They and those who believe their words and keep the commandments of God shall come forth in the first resurrection.

l: the seed of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The seed of the Lord consists of those who have heard and believed the words of the prophets, looked forward to the day of redemption, and those holy prophets who have prophesied. They are heirs of the kingdom of God.

l: kingdom of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The kingdom of God is inherited by the seed of the Lord, including those who believe the prophets and look forward to the remission of their sins.

l: Zion, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Zion is associated with the declaration that the Lord reigns. The Lord shall bring again Zion, and his watchmen shall see eye to eye when this occurs.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Jerusalem is told to break forth into joy because the Lord has comforted and redeemed his people. Waste places of Jerusalem are called to sing together.

l: redemption, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The redemption of the Lord's people was prepared from the foundation of the world. Without it, all mankind must have perished; through it, the Lord satisfies the demands of justice and grants salvation.

l: the crucifixion and death of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Son shall be led, crucified, and slain, with the flesh becoming subject to death and the will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father. Through this death, he takes upon himself iniquity and transgressions and redeems his people.

l: the first resurrection, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The first resurrection includes all the prophets, those who believed their words, those who kept the commandments of God, those who died before Christ came in ignorance without salvation being declared to them, and little children. Those who wilfully rebel against God and die in their sins have no part in it.

l: the resurrection of the dead, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Son has power over the dead and brings to pass the resurrection of the dead. A first resurrection comes before the resurrection of Christ and includes those who shall dwell with God through Christ.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Salvation is granted through the Lord's redemption and shall be declared to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people. It comes to none who wilfully rebel against God, know his commandments, and refuse to keep them.

l: eternal life, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Eternal life is given through Christ to those who are redeemed and have part in the first resurrection. Little children also have eternal life.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Son bears the sins and transgressions of those he redeems. Those who wilfully rebel against God and die in their sins are not redeemed and have no part in the first resurrection.

l: justice, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Son stands between the children of men and justice, takes upon himself their iniquity and transgressions, and satisfies the demands of justice. The Lord cannot deny justice when it has its claim.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: Those who have kept the commandments of God shall come forth in the first resurrection. Those who know the commandments of God and wilfully refuse to keep them have no part in the first resurrection.

l: peace, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The prophets and others publish peace and bring good tidings of good and salvation. The Lord is the founder of peace and those who publish peace are described as having beautiful feet upon the mountains.

l: bands of death, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 15
s: The Son breaks the bands of death and gains victory over death. Having broken them, he has power over the dead and brings to pass the resurrection of the dead.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Abinadi teaches that all nations will see the salvation of the Lord and confess that God's judgments are just. He explains that all mankind became carnal, sensual, and devilish through the fall, but God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state. Christ's coming into the world, his rising from the dead, and the resurrection overcome the grave and the sting of death. The dead will be judged according to their works, receiving either endless life and happiness or endless damnation. Abinadi teaches that redemption comes through Christ the Lord and calls people to repent while the arms of mercy are extended.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: The Lord will bring a time when all nations, kindreds, tongues, and peoples see the salvation of the Lord and confess that his judgments are just. The Lord does not redeem those who refuse to hearken unto his voice.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: God's judgments are confessed to be just. God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state and will judge the dead according to their works.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Christ makes redemption possible and overcomes the grave and the sting of death through his rising from the dead. Redemption comes through Christ the Lord, who is the very Eternal Father.

l: the devil, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: The devil has power over those who remain carnal and rebellious, and he subjected them through their carnal wills and desires. The devil is an enemy to God and will receive those delivered up to him in endless damnation.

l: all mankind, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: All mankind became carnal, sensual, and devilish, knowing evil from good and subjecting themselves to the devil. All mankind would have been endlessly lost without God's redemption.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: The salvation of the Lord will be seen by every nation, kindred, tongue, and people, who will confess before God that his judgments are just.

l: the Fall of Adam, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: The fall was caused by the old serpent beguiling the first parents. It was the cause of all mankind becoming carnal, sensual, and devilish.

l: carnality, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Carnality keeps people in a fallen state when they persist in their own carnal nature and follow sin and rebellion against God. Such people are as though no redemption had been made and remain enemies to God.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Those who continue in sin and rebellion against God remain in a fallen state. People are warned of their iniquities and commanded to repent of their sins.

l: redemption, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Redemption comes through Christ, and God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state. Without Christ's coming into the world there could have been no redemption.

l: Christ's coming into the world, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: If Christ had not come into the world, there could have been no redemption.

l: the resurrection of the dead, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: There is a resurrection because Christ rose from the dead and broke the bands of death. The resurrection brings the dead to stand before the bar of God to be judged according to their works.

l: death, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Christ broke the bands of death so that the grave would have no victory and death would have no sting. Death is swallowed up in Christ, and Christ's life is endless so that there can be no more death.

l: the light of the world, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Christ is the light of the world, an endless light that can never be darkened.

l: eternal life, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Those whose works are good will receive the resurrection of endless life and happiness.

l: Final Judgment, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: The mortal and corrupt will be brought before the bar of God and judged according to their works, whether good or evil. God's judgments are just.

l: everlasting punishment, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: Those whose works are evil will receive the resurrection of endless damnation. They are delivered up to the devil because they followed their carnal wills and refused the Lord's mercy and commands to repent.

l: mercy, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: The arms of mercy were extended toward those who were warned of their iniquities, but they would not depart from them. They would not call upon the Lord while the arms of mercy were extended.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 16
s: People are called to tremble and repent of their sins because they can be saved only in and through Christ. They were commanded to repent, but some would not repent.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi is brought before king Noah after being imprisoned and accused, and he refuses to recall his testimony that God himself should come down among the children of men. Alma believes Abinadi, pleads for him, is cast out, and records Abinadi’s words while hiding. King Noah delivers Abinadi to the priests, who bind and scourge him with faggots until he dies by fire. Before his death, Abinadi prophesies affliction and death by fire for the seed of those who destroy God’s people because they believe in the salvation of the Lord their God.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi refuses to recall the words he has spoken concerning this people and accepts suffering, even death, rather than deny them. He is bound, scourged with faggots, and put to death by fire after prophesying against those who destroy God’s people.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Alma, a young descendant of Nephi, believes Abinadi’s words and pleads with king Noah not to be angry with him. Alma is cast out, pursued by servants, and hides while writing all the words Abinadi had spoken.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: King Noah commands that Abinadi be taken and put to death, then imprisons and questions him. He briefly considers releasing Abinadi because he fears his words and the judgments of God, but the priests stir him to anger and he delivers Abinadi to be slain.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: God is identified as the one whose judgments king Noah fears. Abinadi teaches that God himself should come down among the children of men and that God executes vengeance upon those who destroy his people.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: The priests advise king Noah concerning Abinadi and accuse him of reviling the king. They oppose releasing him, and Abinadi is ultimately delivered to be slain.

l: this people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: This people is the subject of Abinadi’s testimony concerning iniquity. Abinadi says the words spoken against this people are true and will stand as a testimony against them.

l: seed, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi says that the seed of those who put him to death will cause many to suffer the pains of death by fire because they believe in the salvation of the Lord their God.

l: words of Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi’s words concern the iniquity of this people and the coming of God among the children of men. He refuses to recall them, and Alma writes all the words Abinadi had spoken.

l: bonds of iniquity, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi has testified against the iniquity of this people. Their iniquities are said to bring affliction with all manner of diseases.

l: death by fire, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Death by fire is the manner in which Abinadi is put to death. He prophesies that the seed of those responsible will also suffer the pains of death by fire.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: The salvation of the Lord their God is believed in by those whom Abinadi says will suffer death by fire.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi is put to death because he will not deny the commandments of God.

l: truth, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 17
s: Abinadi seals the truth of his words by his death. His words are to stand as a testimony against king Noah and this people at the last day.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma repented, taught Abinadi’s words privately, and gathered believers at Mormon to teach repentance, redemption, and faith in the Lord. He baptized about two hundred and four people, organized them as the church of God or church of Christ, and ordained priests to teach and serve. The people covenanted to serve God, keep his commandments, support one another, and stand as witnesses of God. After the king accused Alma of stirring rebellion, the king’s army pursued Alma and the people, who departed into the wilderness with their families.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma repented of his sins and iniquities after fleeing from the servants of king Noah. He taught Abinadi’s words privately, baptized believers, organized the church, ordained priests, and led the people into the wilderness when the king’s army came to destroy them.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: King Noah’s servants searched for Alma and the people who believed him. The king accused Alma of stirring up the people to rebellion and sent his army to destroy them.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma taught the words of Abinadi concerning what was to come, the resurrection of the dead, and the redemption of the people through Christ.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Christ’s power, sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven were taught as the means through which the people would be redeemed. Baptism was performed through the redemption of Christ.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: God was the object of the people’s covenant, service, worship, gratitude, and witness. Alma taught that God could redeem them, number them with those of the first resurrection, and grant eternal life through Christ.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma taught faith on the Lord and repentance. The people were baptized in the name of the Lord, gathered to worship the Lord, observed the sabbath, and gave thanks to the Lord their God.

l: Spirit of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The Spirit of the Lord came upon Alma when he prayed before baptizing Helam. Alma and Helam arose from the water filled with the Spirit, and the people were filled with the grace of God.

l: people who believed Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The people who believed Alma went to Mormon to hear his teachings. They were baptized, became members of the church, covenanted to serve God and keep his commandments, supported one another, and departed into the wilderness with Alma.

l: Alma's people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The people of the Lord were warned of the coming of the king’s army. They took their tents and families and departed into the wilderness.

l: church of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The baptized people were called the church of God from that time forward. Whoever was baptized by the power and authority of God was added to the church.

l: church of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The baptized people were also called the church of Christ from that time forward. The church was taught to have unity, love, one faith, and one baptism.

l: priests, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma ordained one priest for every fifty people to preach and teach the things pertaining to the kingdom of God. The priests were commanded to labor with their own hands, receive the grace of God, and serve without depending on the people for support.

l: king's army, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The king’s army was sent to destroy Alma and the people because the king accused Alma of stirring up rebellion. Alma and the people departed into the wilderness before the army arrived.
